title: Short codes for common letters
hook: 8 letters, 2 bits each, 16 bits. Can uneven codes do better?

doesNotKnow: that codes can have different lengths and still be decoded

misconception: Every symbol needs the same number of bits, so 8 symbols from 4 kinds always cost 16 bits.
objective: The learner can explain that each join adds one bit to every symbol beneath it, so joining the two rarest groups first gives common symbols short codes and rare ones long codes, and the message 4A 2B 1C 1D needs 14 bits instead of 16.

claims.text: Joining C + D, then that with B, then with A gives code lengths A 1, B 2, C 3, D 3, for 4x1 + 2x2 + 1x3 + 1x3 = 14 bits; the Bits readout shows the same total as the join costs 2 + 4 + 8 = 14.
claims.source: Each symbol's code length is its depth in the tree. Equivalently each join adds its weight: 2 + 4 + 8 = 14. Builder computed both in Node. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node port of join()/lightest() (fc22-5/huff.mjs): two presses of 'Join the two rarest' give (CD), then ((CD)B) and the automatic join with A; joins 2 + 4 + 8 = 14; codes C 000, D 001, B 01, A 1, so lengths 1,2,3,3 and 4+4+3+3 = 14. Bits readout text is joins.join(' + ') + ' = 14'.

claims.text: Giving each of the 8 letters a 2-digit code costs 16 bits.
claims.source: 8 symbols x 2 bits = 16. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 11): Message is 4 A + 2 B + 1 C + 1 D = 8 letters; 8 x 2 = 16 (matches FIXED = 16 in Demo.tsx and the predict text).

claims.text: Each join puts one more digit on the code of every letter inside it, so a join costs the group's total count in bits.
claims.source: A join makes the two groups children of a new node, lengthening every code beneath by one bit (0 for one side, 1 for the other). Total bits = sum over symbols of weight x depth = sum over joins of the joined weight. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 11): Total bits = sum weight x depth; each merge adds 1 to the depth of every leaf beneath it, so sum over merges of merged weight is the same total. For 4,2,1,1: merges 2 + 4 + 8 = 14.

claims.text: In a code read off such a tree, no code starts another, so a message can be decoded without gaps.
claims.source: Codes are the paths to leaves; a leaf has no descendants, so no codeword is a prefix of another (prefix code). CLRS 3rd ed., 16.3 'Huffman codes'. Example from the brief's tree: 1, 01, 000, 001. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 11): Codewords are root-to-leaf paths and leaves have no children, so no codeword is a prefix of another; brief codes 1, 01, 000, 001 checked prefix-free.

claims.text: Huffman proved that always joining the two rarest groups gives the fewest bits possible for any code where no code starts another.
claims.source: Huffman, 'A Method for the Construction of Minimum-Redundancy Codes', Proc. IRE 40(9), 1952; optimality proof in CLRS 3rd ed., 16.3, Lemmas 16.2-16.3 and Theorem 16.4. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 11): Huffman 1952, Proc. IRE 40(9):1098-1101; optimality among prefix codes is CLRS 3rd ed. Thm 16.4 (greedy choice Lemma 16.2, optimal substructure Lemma 16.3). Claim limits itself to prefix codes: correct.

claims.text: With two groups left, only one join is possible, so the stage makes it automatically (the caption says so when three groups remain: "Join two of these. The last two then join on their own.").
claims.source: Demo.tsx join(): when the forest has two trees they are joined; any order gives the same total because the last join always costs the full weight (8). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): join() in Demo.tsx: when next.length === 2 it merges the two at once, so the forest goes 4 -> 3 -> 1 and is never left at 2. The caption 'Join two of these. The last two then join on their own.' shows when forest.length is 3 (not 4, not done, nothing selected, not in the 10-bit view). Every manual order ends with a join of 8 (all 10 distinct totals enumerated).

claims.text: The tree you build by joining C + D, then B, then A gives the codes A 1, B 01, C 000, D 001.
claims.source: Demo.tsx joins (C,D), then (CD,B), then (CDB,A), labelling the left child 0 and the right 1: A is the right child of the root (1), B the right child of the left subtree (01), C and D are 000 and 001. Lengths 1, 2, 3, 3 match c1.

claims.text: The codes A 0, B 1, C 00, D 01 cost 4x1 + 2x1 + 1x2 + 1x2 = 10 bits, but A's 0 starts C's 00, so "00" could be C or A A and the message cannot be decoded without gaps.
claims.source: SHORT and SHORT_BITS in Demo.tsx: 4 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10. The string 00 parses as C (00) or as A A (0, 0); likewise 01 parses as D or A B. So the code set is not uniquely decodable. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): SHORT_BITS recomputed: 4x1 + 2x1 + 1x2 + 1x2 = 10. '00' parses as C or A A, '01' as D or A B, so the set is not uniquely decodable. Stage message: '10 bits, but is "00" C, or A then A? A's 0 starts C's 00.'

recall.question: Building a Huffman code, which two groups do you join first?
options: Any two neighbours in the alphabet
recall.why: Every join adds a bit to each symbol beneath it. Joining the rarest first puts the extra bits where they are used least, leaving common symbols with short codes.
